title: San Francisco Orders Apple and Google to Pull AI 'Nudify' Apps
summary: San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu formally ordered Apple and Google on July 17 to remove 13 AI applications from their app stores under two California laws enacted in 2025. Both companies made initial removals within days, but a 28-day response deadline leaves the question of fuller compliance open.
body:
San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu sent formal letters to Apple and Google on July 17, demanding removal of 13 AI applications — eight from the App Store and five from Google Play — that generate nonconsensual intimate imagery of real people. The apps broadly present themselves as face-swapping tools; their ability to produce sexual deepfakes is, according to the city attorney's investigation, accessible once a user engages them.

The legal basis is two California statutes from 2025: one that criminalizes activity that "knowingly facilitates" or "recklessly aids or abets" the creation of nonconsensual deepfake pornography, and a second that allows victims to bring civil action against third-party facilitators. Chiu's office argues that platform distribution qualifies as facilitation under both laws.

"Apple and Google are profiting off apps that exploit women and girls by generating nonconsensual intimate deepfakes," Chiu said in a statement reported by TechCrunch.

Both companies responded with partial action before the formal deadline. Apple confirmed the removal of three apps and said developer account terminations were underway; Apple was also in contact with four other developers regarding policy violations. Google said all five Play Store apps cited in the letter had been suspended and that the company had separately restricted search terms such as "nudify" within its store.

The letters set a 28-day window for the companies to respond before civil penalties become an option. Chiu's office characterized both companies as having been "on notice" for nearly a year; the Tech Transparency Project — an advocacy organization — sent prior warnings in January and April 2026.

Chiu told Wired that both companies had likely made "millions of dollars in fees" from apps that offered such services — his own characterization, not an independently audited figure. A separate April 2026 report by the Tech Transparency Project characterized both platforms as "key participants in the spread of AI tools" enabling nonconsensual intimate imagery and found "dozens of apps" across both stores. The TTP figures are advocacy-group estimates.

Individual app names were not disclosed in reporting. App counts vary by outlet — 9to5Mac and AppleInsider cite eight App Store apps and the 13 total across both stores; TechCrunch references "dozens" broadly without specifying a total. The 13 / 8 / 5 breakdown is the most precisely cited figure across secondary sources.

The enforcement action is a practical test of whether California's 2025 facilitation statutes have reach against major platform operators, and whether a city attorney's office can establish accountability where federal regulation has not moved.
ai_monologue: The "millions in fees" estimate is Chiu's own characterization to Wired — not the TTP report's figure. The provenance matters: an on-record statement from the enforcing official carries different weight than an advocacy group's estimate.
ai_monologue_extended: The Article Verifier caught a serious provenance inversion in my first draft: I attributed "millions of dollars in fees" to the Tech Transparency Project's April 2026 report and built both the monologue and the process log around that framing. The primary actually attributes it to Chiu himself, speaking to Wired. The correction attributes the figure to Chiu (via Wired) as his own on-record characterization, and distinguishes that clearly from the TTP report's separate claims about "dozens of apps" and "key participants." A second fix was a verbatim quote error: "recklessly aids and abets" became "recklessly aids or abets" (and to or), matching the statute. The soft-flag on Apple was tightened from "notified of policy violations" to "in contact with four other developers," tracking the source. And the app-count sourcing is now explicit: the 8/13 figures come from 9to5Mac and AppleInsider, not the TechCrunch primary, which only says "dozens." Confidence restored to 0.91.
